penetration_assumption: The ₹5.26 L is NOT new assortment — it is the existing 218-SKU range actually being on the shelf. Assumption in plain words: on 42 of 354 trading days, 8 of the top-10 snack SKUs were available and the shop sold ₹12.55 of snacks per bill; on the 45 worst days only 0-4 were available and it sold ₹9.47-10.78 per bill, at IDENTICAL footfall (998 vs 997 bills/day), so the gradient is availability and not traffic. If every day ran at the already-achieved ₹12.55/bill across the 372,341 bills the shop actually rang, snacks do ₹46.73 L instead of ₹41.47 L = ₹5.26 L gross uplift. At the live-derived 10.65% gross margin that is ₹56,000 of gross profit. Extrapolation stays inside the observed range — I did not model a 10-of-10 day because zero such days exist. SEPARATE and EXCLUDED from the headline: the one genuinely untested assortment line is health/baked snacks (26 Too Yumm SKUs listed and never purchased once, not one unit ever). Assumption there: if 3% of the ~4,700 residents (about 140 people) buy one ₹20 baked/health pack twice a month, that is 140 x 2 x 12 x ₹20 = ₹67,200/yr gross, roughly half cannibalised from Lays. It needs a purchase order against codes that already exist, not a new SKU line — which is why sku_lines_to_add is 0.

kill_reason: Not a kill — but the ASSORTMENT half of the question is a false gap and must not be funded. ARY lists 723 active snack SKUs and buys only 218 of them; the estimated benchmark for a 5,000-person store's chips/extruded/namkeen sub-tree is ~200 lines (BigBasket metro pro-rated at the benchmark lane's own 0.159 ratio — ESTIMATED), so the range is already at or above benchmark. Of the 498 dormant SKUs, ZERO were purchased in the last 12 months, only 1 holds any stock, and 281 were never purchased in the database's entire history — they are catalogue noise, not an opportunity and not trapped capital (₹56,119 total). The real defect is mechanical and verified: 1 of 723 snack SKUs has a ReorderLevel set, 0 have a SafetyLevel, 0 have the reorder flag on. Stock on hand is ₹56,119 at cost = 6.2 days of cover and 59 turns/yr; snacks are 0.49% of shop stock value while producing 5.4% of sales. The #1 SKU (Lays Kurkure Masala Munch 102g, 13,059 units/yr) holds 84 units = 2.3 days and sold on only 249 of 354 open days. MARGIN TRAP WORTH PROPAGATING TO EVERY OTHER CATEGORY: the naive PurchaseCost-vs-SaleRate comparison gives 19.92%; the true figure is 10.65%, because SaleDetail carries IncludeInRate=true (GST inside FinalSaleAmount) while PurchaseDetail carries IncludeInRate=false (ItemValue excludes recoverable input GST). That 9.3-point error would nearly double any sizing built on it. Whole category throws only ₹3.95 L of gross profit a year, so it cannot pay for much management attention. WHAT STOPS THIS BEING HIGH CONFIDENCE: 'days with a sale' is a proxy for availability — there are no historical daily stock snapshots to confirm a stockout — and the rupees-per-bill gradient could partly reflect reverse causality (a high-snack-appetite day sells more distinct SKUs). Flat footfall between the low bands handles the crude version of that, not the appetite version. The VERDICT (availability, not assortment) is high confidence; the ₹5.26 L figure is medium.

blockers: Supplier reach from Rajgarh HP is the probable root cause, not buyer discipline. 6.2 days of cover on a shop 30-50 km up hill road means the fix needs a bigger safety stock and a firmer delivery cadence from the Lays/Haldiram hill-route distributor — that is a negotiation and working capital, not a config change.

FusionERP8 replenishment is entirely unconfigured for this category: 1 of 723 SKUs has a ReorderLevel, 0 have a SafetyLevel, 0 have the reorder flag on. Someone has to populate reorder points on ~25 SKUs before any ordering rule can fire.

The prize is small in absolute terms. The whole snacks category throws ₹3.95 L of gross profit a year at 10.65%; a perfect availability fix adds ~₹56,000. This cannot justify significant management time — it is a checklist item, not a project.

Seasonality makes safety stock risky. January sales collapsed to ₹1.32 L against a ₹4.41 L September peak (campus vacation). Over-ordering crush-prone nitrogen-flushed chips in December leaves them sitting through an empty campus at 3-4 month shelf life; monsoon humidity at 173101 is the stated write-off driver.

Do NOT read the 498 dormant SKUs as a delisting saving — they hold only ₹56,119 of stock in total across the whole live range, so cleaning them frees almost no capital. The benefit is POS and catalogue hygiene only.

Substitution masks the leak, so the ₹5.26 L will not appear in any report until availability is fixed. Buyers on a closed campus switch flavour rather than walk out, which is why category revenue only sags ~23% per bill on the worst days instead of collapsing.
